d.t: Any nounal word or phrase which indicates a particular person, place, class, or thing.
d.e: I've never liked the name my parents gave me so I changed it at the age of twenty.

d.t: A reputation.
d.e: And David won a name for himself.

d.t: An abusive or insulting epithet.
d.e: Stop calling me names!

d.t: A person (or legal person).
d.e:
p. 2002, second edition of, 2002, Graham Richards, Putting Psychology in its Place, →ISBN, page 287 http://books.google.com/books?id=7bxvJIs5_wsC&pg=PA287&dq=names
Later British psychologists interested in this topic include such major names as Cyril Burt, William McDougall, […] .

d.t: Those of a certain name; a race; a family.
An authority; a behalf.
d.e: Halt in the name of the law!

d.t: (computing) An identifier, generally a unique string of characters.
(UK, finance) An investor in Lloyd's of London bearing unlimited liability.
Any of several types of true yam (Dioscorea) used in Caribbean Spanish cooking.
(ditransitive) To give a name to.
d.e: One visitor named Hou Yugang said he was not too concerned about climate change and Baishui’s melting.

d.t: (transitive) To mention, specify.
d.e: He named his demands.

d.t: (transitive) To identify as relevant or important
d.e: naming the problem

d.t: (transitive) To publicly implicate by name.
d.e: The painter was named as an accomplice.

d.t: (transitive, of a person) To disclose the name of.
d.e: Police are not naming the suspect as he is a minor.

d.t: (transitive) To designate for a role.
d.e: My neighbor was named to the steering committee.

d.t: (transitive, Westminster system politics) To initiate a process to temporarily remove a member of parliament who is breaking the rules of conduct.
Existing in nature.
Pertaining to birth or descent; native.
(now rare) A native inhabitant of a place, country, etc.
(music) A note that is not or is no longer to be modified by an accidental.
(music) The symbol ♮ used to indicate such a natural note.
One with an innate talent at or for something.
d.e: He's a natural on the saxophone.

d.t: (uncountable) An almost white colour, with tints of grey, yellow or brown; originally that of natural fabric.
(archaic) One with a simple mind; a fool or idiot.
(colloquial, chiefly UK) One's life.
(US, colloquial) A hairstyle for people with Afro-textured hair in which the hair is not straightened or otherwise treated.
(chiefly in the plural, slang) A breast which has not been modified by plastic surgery.
d.e: big naturals

d.t: (bodybuilding) Someone who has not used anabolic steroids or other performance-enhancing substances.
(craps) A roll of two dice with a score of 7 or 11 on the comeout roll.
(baccarat) A deal of cards totalling 8 or 9.
(colloquial, dialect) Naturally; in a natural manner.
Physically close.
d.e: I can't see near objects very clearly without my glasses.

d.t: Close in time.
d.e: The end is near.

d.t: Closely connected or related.
d.e: The deceased man had no near relatives.

d.t: Close to one's interests, affection, etc.; intimate; dear.
d.e: It is a matter of near consequence to me.

d.t: Close to anything followed or imitated; not free, loose, or rambling.
d.e: a version near to the original

d.t: So as barely to avoid or pass injury or loss; close; narrow.
d.e: a near escape

d.t: Approximate, almost.
d.e: The two words are near synonyms.

d.t: (UK, in relation to a vehicle) On the side nearest to the kerb (the left-hand side if one drives on the left).
d.e: The near front wheel came loose.

d.t: (dated) Next to the driver, when he is on foot; (US) on the left of an animal or a team.
d.e: the near ox; the near leg

d.t: (obsolete) Immediate; direct; close; short.
(now rare) Stingy; parsimonious.
d.e: Don't be near with your pocketbook.

d.t: (programming, not comparable) Within the currently selected segment in a segmented memory architecture.
d.e: a near pointer

d.t: At or towards a position close in space or time.
Nearly; almost.
d.e: He was near unconscious when I found him.

d.t: Physically close to, in close proximity to.
d.e: There are habitable planets orbiting many of the stars near our Sun.

d.t: Close to in time.
d.e: The voyage was near completion.

d.t: Close to in nature or degree.
d.e: His opinions are near the limit of what is acceptable.

d.t: (ambitransitive) To come closer to; to approach.
d.e: The ship nears the land.

d.t: The left side of a horse or of a team of horses pulling a carriage etc.
(dialectal, rare, Lincolnshire, Derbyshire) Kidney.
(countable and uncountable) A requirement for something; something needed.
d.e: There's no need to speculate; we can easily find out for sure.

d.t: A desire or craving for the satisfaction of a requirement perceived as essential or primal.
Lack of means of subsistence; poverty; indigence; destitution.
(transitive) To have an absolute requirement for.
d.e: Living things need water to survive.

d.t: (transitive) To want strongly; to feel that one must have something.
d.e: After ten days of hiking, I needed a shower and a shave.

d.t: (modal, chiefly in the negative and interrogative) To be obliged or required (to do something).
d.e: I need not go if I don't want to, need I?

d.t: (intransitive) To be required; to be necessary.
(obsolete, transitive) To be necessary (to someone).
At no time; on no occasion; in no circumstance.
d.e: I finally finished, and I never do wanna do it again.

d.t: Not at any other time; not on any other occasion; not previously.
d.e:
1908, Lucy Maud Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables, Chapter XIII: The Delights of Anticipation,
I never saw such an infatuated man.

d.t: (colloquial) Negative particle (used to negate verbs in the simple past tense; also used absolutely).
d.e: The police say I stole the car, but I never did it.

d.t: (Manglish, Singlish, auxiliary) Did not; didn't.
A statement of defiance
d.e: ‘Guess what, I've won the pools!’ ‘Never!’

d.t: Recently made, or created.
d.e: This is a new scratch on my car! The band just released a new album.

d.t: Additional; recently discovered.
d.e: We turned up some new evidence from the old files.

d.t: Current or later, as opposed to former.
d.e: My new car is much better than my previous one, even though it is older. We had been in our new house for five years by then.

d.t: Used to distinguish something established more recently, named after something or some place previously existing.
d.e: New Bond Street is an extension of Bond Street.

d.t: In original condition; pristine; not previously worn or used.
d.e: Are you going to buy a new car or a second-hand one?

d.t: Refreshed, reinvigorated, reformed.
d.e: That shirt is dirty. Go and put on a new one. I feel like a new person after a good night's sleep. After the accident, I saw the world with new eyes.

d.t: Newborn.
d.e: My sister has a new baby, and our mother is excited to finally have a grandchild.

d.t: Strange, unfamiliar or not previously known.
d.e: The idea was new to me. I need to meet new people.

d.t: Recently arrived or appeared.
d.e: Have you met the new guy in town? He is the new kid at school.

d.t: Inexperienced or unaccustomed at some task.
d.e: Don't worry that you're new at this job; you'll get better with time. I'm new at this business, I'm still new to the work.

d.t: (of a period of time) Next; about to begin or recently begun.
d.e: We expect to grow at 10% annually in the new decade.

d.t: Synonym of newly, especially in composition.
d.e: Near-synonym: recently

d.t: As new; from scratch.
d.e: They are scraping the site clean to build new.

d.t: (with the, invariable plural only) Things that are new.
d.e: Out with the old, in with the new.

d.t: (Australia, uncountable) A typically light-coloured lager brewed by the bottom-fermentation method.
(UK, naval slang, countable) A naval cadet who has just embarked on training.
(programming) Synonym of new up.
(obsolete) To make new; to recreate; to renew.
Nearest in place or position, having nothing similar intervening; adjoining.
d.e: The man in the next bunk kept me awake all night with his snoring.

d.t: Nearest in order, succession, or rank; immediately following (or sometimes preceding) in order.
d.e: Please turn to the next page.

d.t: (chiefly law) Nearest in relationship. (See also next of kin.)
d.e: next friend

d.t: Denotes the one immediately following the current or most recent one.
d.e: Next week would be a good time to meet.

d.t: (of days of the week or months of the year) Closest in the future, or closest but one if the closest is very soon; of days, sometimes thought to specifically refer to the instance closest to seven days (one week) in the future.
d.e: The party is next Tuesday; that is, not tomorrow, but eight days from now.

d.t: In a time, place, rank or sequence closest or following.
d.e: They live in the next closest house.

d.t: On the first subsequent occasion.
d.e: Financial panic, earthquakes, oil spills, riots. What comes next?

d.t: (obsolete or poetic) On the side of; nearest or adjacent to; next to.
d.e: The fact that the line cannot be original is patent from the fact that Aias in the rest of the Iliad is not encamped next the Athenians […] .

d.t: The one that follows after this one.
d.e: Next, please, don't hold up the queue!

d.t: (gaming) Next match
d.e: gg team, Wanna play next?

d.t: (countable) The time when the Sun is below the horizon when the sky is dark.
d.e: Most animals are awake at day and sleep at night.

d.t: (astronomy, countable) The period of darkness beginning at the end of evening astronomical twilight when the sun is 18 degrees below the horizon, and ending at the beginning of morning astronomical twilight.
(law, countable) A period of time often defined in the legal system as beginning 30 minutes after sunset, and ending 30 minutes before sunrise.
(countable) An evening or night spent at a particular activity.
d.e: a night on the town

d.t: (countable) A day, or at least a night.
d.e: I stayed my friend's house for three nights.

d.t: (uncountable) Nightfall.
d.e: from noon till night

d.t: (uncountable) Darkness (due to it being nighttime).
d.e: The cat disappeared into the night.

d.t: (uncountable) A dark blue colour, midnight blue.
(sports, colloquial) A night's worth of competitions, generally one game.
Ellipsis of good night.
d.e: Night, y'all! Thanks for a great evening!

d.t: (intransitive) To spend a night (in a place), to overnight.
Not any.
d.e: no one

d.t: Hardly any.
d.e: We'll be finished in no time at all.

d.t: Not any possibility or allowance of (something).
d.e: No smoking. No parking.

d.t: Not (a); not properly, not really; not fully.
d.e: My mother's no fool.

d.t: (with following adjective) Not, not at all.
(without adjective, now Scotland, informal) Not.
d.e: I just want to find out whether she's coming or no.

d.t: (colloquial, usually humorous) Not, does not, do not, etc.
d.e: Ug no like veggie.

d.t: (archaic) Alternative form of No.
Used to show disagreement, negation, denial, refusal, or prohibition.
d.e: No, you are mistaken.

d.t: Used to ask for confirmation.
d.e: The legal drinking age in the States is 21, no?

d.t: Used to express sadness or disappointment.
d.e: "We lost." "No!"

d.t: Used to express disbelief.
d.e: I got the job! / No! Really? That's fantastic!

d.t: Used to show agreement with a negative question.
d.e: "Don’t you like milk?" "No." (i.e., "No, I don’t like milk.")

d.t: (colloquial) Used together with an affirmative word or phrase to show agreement.
d.e: No, totally.

d.t: Without.
d.e: Look Ma, no hands!

d.t: Like.
A negating expression; an answer that shows disagreement, denial, refusal, or disapproval.
A vote not in favor, or opposing a proposition.
d.e: The workers voted on whether to strike, and there were thirty yeses and two nos.

d.t: Alternative form of No.
(intransitive, colloquial) To say “no”.
(transitive, colloquial) To answer with “no”; to decline, reject.
Not anymore; no more.
d.e: no longer with us

d.t: Negates the meaning of the modified verb.
d.e: Did you take out the trash? — No, I did not. I do not think it was my turn, was it?

d.t: To no degree.
d.e: That is not red; it's green.

d.t: (litotes) Used to indicate the opposite or near opposite, often in a form of understatement.
d.e: That day was not the best day of my life. (meaning the day was bad or awful)

d.t: Used before a determiner phrase, a pronominal phrase etc. to convey a negative attitude (e.g. denial, sadness, anger) towards something.
d.e: Oh god, not that! Anything but that!

d.t: (ironic, informal, originally African-American Vernacular) Used before a non-finite clause (especially a gerund-participial clause) or less commonly a determiner phrase to ironically convey some attitude (e.g. surprise, incredulity, amusement, or embarrassment) towards something.
d.e: Not me writing example sentences again.

d.t: And not.
d.e: I wanted a plate of shrimp, not a bucket of chicken.

d.t: (slang) Used to indicate that the previous phrase was meant sarcastically or ironically.
d.e: Near-synonyms: I don't think; psych; bender (obsolete, UK)

d.t: An instance of using the word "not"; a negation or denial.
Alternative letter-case form of NOT (“unary operation on logical values that changes true to false, and false to true”).
A symbol or annotation.
A written or printed communication or commitment.
(music) A sound.
(perfumery) An element of a scent, fragrance, or perfume, especially as a descriptor or category.
(uncountable) Observation; notice; heed.
(uncountable) Reputation; distinction.
d.e: a poet of note

d.t: A critical comment.
d.e: Your performance was fantastic! I have just one note: you were a little flat in bars 35 and 36.

d.t: (obsolete) Notification; information; intelligence.
(obsolete) Mark of disgrace.
(uncountable) That which is needed or necessary; business; duty; work.
d.e: Tha'll keep me at this noit all day... Om always at this noit.

d.t: Milk-giving by a cow or sow; (specifically) the period following calving or farrowing, during which a cow or sow is most productive and useful.
(by extension) The milk given by a cow or sow during such period.
(transitive) To notice with care; to observe; to remark; to heed.
d.e: If you look to the left, you can note the old cathedral.

d.t: (transitive) To record in writing; to make a memorandum of.
d.e: We noted his speech.

d.t: (transitive) To denote; to designate.
d.e: The modular multiplicative inverse of x may be noted x⁻¹.

d.t: (transitive) To annotate.
(transitive) To set down in musical characters.
(transitive, law) To record on the back of (a bill, draft, etc.) a refusal of acceptance, as the ground of a protest, which is done officially by a notary.
d.e: By noting the protest, notaries could date certificates when they were received, making it easier to comply with time restrictions associated with protesting.

d.t: Not any thing; no thing.
d.e: Don't just say nothing. Tell me what's going on.

d.t: An absence of anything, including empty space, brightness, darkness, matter, or a vacuum.
Something trifling, or of no consequence or importance.
d.e:
- What happened to your face?
- It's nothing.

d.t: A trivial remark especially in the term sweet nothings.
A nobody (insignificant person).
(archaic) Not at all; in no way.
d.e: Nothing too much out of the ordinary.

d.t: (colloquial) Used to dismiss a previous statement.
d.e:
- Wait a moment.
- Wait nothing! I'm going after them.

d.t: Completely unimportant.
d.e: Dallas scored on what had seemed until then like a nothing play.

d.t: Lacking effort or commitment.
d.e: The cricketer played a nothing shot.

d.t: Never mind; it's not important; forget what I said.
Present; current.
d.e: […] to my now wife Mabell, my child Elisabeth, & my child now begotten, &c., and they to be joint Exõrs, & if all die, then the same jointly to my brother William Every & my sisters Sarah Skibbowe & Joan Brice.

d.t: (informal) Fashionable; popular; up to date; current.
d.e: I think this band's sound is very now.

d.t: At the present time.
d.e: Now I am six.

d.t: (sentential) Used to introduce a point, a qualification of what has previously been said, a remonstration or a rebuke.
d.e: Now, we all want what is best for our children.

d.t: Differently from the immediate past; differently from a more remote past or a possible future; differently from all other times.
d.e: Now I am ready.

d.t: At the time reached within a narration.
d.e: Now he remembered why he had come.

d.t: Used to indicate a context of urgency.
d.e: Now listen, we must do something about this.

d.t: (informal) At the present point of a recurring cycle or event.
d.e: I always used to do my shopping now, to avoid the rush.

d.t: (obsolete, as but now) Very recently; not long ago; up to the present.
(usually emphasized) Used to address a switching side, or sharp change in attitude from before.
d.e: Now, you want to protect me. An hour ago, you were mercilessly bullying me!

d.t: Sometimes; occasionally; used to list a series of often assumed states.
d.e: His face fit his roles: now smiling, now earnest, now glowering, now raging.

d.t: (often with that) Since, because, in light of the fact.
d.e: Now all the children have grown up and left, the house is very quiet.

d.t: Indicates a signal to begin.
d.e: Now! Fire all we've got while the enemy is in reach!

d.t: (uncountable) The present time.
d.e: Now is the right time.

d.t: (often with the) The state of not paying attention to the future or the past.
d.e: She is living in the now.

d.t: (countable, chiefly in phenomenology) A particular instant in time, as perceived at that instant.
Misspelling of know.
d.e: I don't now.

d.t: Quantity of countable things.
d.e: Any number of people can be reading from a given repository at a time.

d.t: (countable) An abstract entity used to describe quantity.
d.e: Zero, one, −1, 2.5, and pi are all numbers.

d.t: (countable) A numeral: a symbol for a non-negative integer.
d.e: The number 8 is usually made with a single stroke.

d.t: (countable, mathematics) An element of one of several sets: natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, complex numbers, and sometimes extensions such as hypercomplex numbers, etc.
d.e: The equation e#123;i#92;pi#125;#43;1#61;0 includes the most important numbers: 1, 0, #92;pi, i, and e.

d.t: (Followed by a numeral; used attributively) Indicating the position of something in a list or sequence. Abbreviations: No or No., no or no. (in each case, sometimes written with a superscript "o", like Nº or №). The symbol "#" is also used in this manner.
d.e: Horse number 5 won the race.

d.t: A sequence of digits and letters used to register people, automobiles, and various other items.
d.e: Her passport number is C01X864TN.

d.t: (countable, informal) A telephone number.
d.e: Let's give her a call. Do you have her number handy?

d.t: (grammar) Of a word or phrase, the state of being singular, dual or plural, shown by inflection.
d.e: Adjectives and nouns should agree in gender, number, and case.

d.t: (now rare, in the plural) Poetic metres; verses, rhymes.
(countable) A performance; especially, a single song or song and dance routine within a larger show.
d.e: For his second number, he sang "The Moon Shines Bright".

d.t: (singular only, formal) A group of people.
d.e: I include myself in their number.

d.t: (countable, informal) A person.
Something that numbs.
(intransitive) To total or count; to amount to.
d.e: I don’t know how many books are in the library, but they must number in the thousands.

d.t: (transitive, passive voice) To limit to a certain number; to reckon (as by fate) to be few in number.
d.e: The old man knew that his days were numbered.

d.t: (transitive, literary or archaic) To count; to determine the quantity of.
d.e: The king ordered that all his subjects be numbered.

d.t: (transitive) To label (items) with numbers; to assign numbers to (items).
d.e: Number the baskets so that we can find them easily.

d.t: (transitive, with off) To call out and assign a series of numbers (usually to people), either for the sake of dividing into groups or for counting.
d.e: Shelley numbered off the group into two teams for the baseball game.

d.t: (transitive, with off) To enumerate or list, especially while assigning numbers to.
(transitive, usually with among) To classify or include (in a group of things).
d.e: Alexander the Great's army numbered an elite cavalry among its ranks.

d.t: (intransitive, usually with among) To be classified or included (in a certain group or category of things).
d.e: Her horses number among the fastest in her country.

d.t: comparative form of numb: more numb
